posts.text:
In celebration of Jensen Huang's return and his commitment to open-source AI:

Today we’re releasing OCRia-nano-1, an extremely lightweight and open-weight OCR model that is just 8.1M parameters in size and can parse pages at 426 ms per page on your CPU ⚡️ - no GPU required! 

OCRia-nano-1 is intended to be the first pass parsing for the billions of pages/petabytes of data that are locked up within any organization and unlock it for all agentic automation. Even at its size, it still has the following properties:
✅ it can parse complex tables and generate bounding boxes
✅ it is natively multilingual and can cover CJK, right-to-left, and other scripts
✅ is more accurate than Marker, PP-OCRv6, Tesseract while being up to 2-5x faster

It is perfect for ‘unlimited’ high-volume ingestion (e.g. indexing a petabyte scale RAG knowledge base) and ad-hoc uploaded files where the agent has additional tools to inspect the file more deeply. You can always use larger VLMs (like OCRia-1.5) for any document that requires higher visual accuracy.

Best of all, it’s a fully open-weight model available through liteparse. If you’re interested in using it for commercial use, come talk to us!

Blog: https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/introducing-ocria-nano-1

Install OCRia-nano-1 through liteparse: https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse/
Weights on @huggingface: https://huggingface.co/llamaindex/OCRia-nano-1
Full technical report:

posts.text:
I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :)

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

It's deployed here: https://karpathy.ai/usaciv/ and the "?" has the source link too. I don't exactly know where I was going with this but it's really fun to browse and play with. Possibly it can be expanded or built into a game. I only have half of my weekly Claude quote left though so someone else will have to take over :D. Claude also made a trailer:
posts.why_viral: Karpathy shipped a live US Civilization map that Opus 5.5 built in 7 hours and 45K lines from 31 public datasets.
posts.why_it_matters: A concrete ceiling on what Claude Code desktop plus Opus 5.5 can assemble in one session, with the app and source public.
posts.newsletter_title: Claude built a Civilization-style US map from 31 public data sources. 7 hours, 45K lines.

posts.text:
Taking over someone else's unfinished work in 2022:

Open GitHub, there's a PR there.
+673 -241 diff.

Checkout the branch, run tests.
They pass.

Spend 2 hours reading the code to understand it.

There's a weird if statement that you don't understand why it's there.
You ask the coworker who opened the PR.

He says it's because some obscure payload field can be null and now it all makes sense, you understand all the code.

Read the ticket again to see what's missing and write rest of code.

+871 -308 final diff.
Merge PR.

✅ Done.

Taking over someone else's work in 2026:

Open GitHub. There's a PR there.
+87341 -32651 diff.

Tell Claude to read the ticket and see what's left.
Claude comes up with 5 bullet points of what's left to do. You understand none of them.

There are 15 markdown files in the PR your coworker's agent dumped for future context.
You open them. 3000 lines each. You understand none of it.

Ask Claude to explain it like you're 5.
Claude outputs words that are coherent but you still understand none of it.

You tell Claude to make diagrams to explain the architecture.
A tiny bit of it starts making sense.

There's some weird service "Transactional Reconciliation Service" you don't understand why it's there. Claude says it shouldn't be there and the markdown files don't specify why it's there.

You ask the coworker about that service.
He has no idea what you're talking about, he needs to ask his agent.

His Claude makes an artifact that explains why that service is slop that was written by the subagent who implemented it and shouldn't be there at all.

The coworker hands that artifact to you. He hasn't read it.

You hand the artifact to your Claude. Your Claude advices to remove the service and proposes 4 different solutions to replace it.

You understand none of the solutions but there is one which seems to make more sense. You ask the coworker if that's a good call.

He has no idea what any of that means, he asks his agent. His agent says it's a good solution but it's missing an important edge case. He copy pastes the agent output in Slack.

You copy paste the Slack message into your Claude. Your Claude says that you're absolutely right, that this is an important edge case that was not handled in the initial solution. Claude proposes a small fix to cover it and asks if it should implement it along with the other 5 bullet points.

You say ok, Claude starts writing code. PR diff grows to +97564 -41698.

You ask Claude if everything in the ticket is implemented. Claude starts reviewing the code.

Claude says that most of it is implemented, but comes up with 5 bullet points of things that are missing.

You are confused, it already came up with 5 bullet points the first time you asked. These seem different bullet points that only came up after reviewing the code though, so you say ok, implement it.

Claude writes code.
PR +102467 -45790 diff.

You ask if now it's all done.
Claude reviews the code. Says it's mostly done but there 3 low priority items that are not yet implemented.

You don't understand any of the items but since they're low priority you figure out they don't matter much, so you click merge.

PR spends 3 hours in the merge queue for CI to go green, then it merges.

Next Monday your coworker asks his agent to deploy to AWS.
Your agent's code now runs in production.

2 hours later the whole backend is down. No one knows why.

Your coworker asks his agent to investigate. After 20 minutes it finds the code that threw an unhandled error when some payload came up with an obscure null field.

Your coworker doesn't recognize any of that code and his agent says it should not be there but you wrote it so your coworker should check with you first.

He asks you about that code.

You've never seen that code in your entire life.
You ask your agent about it.

Your Claude says the error was thrown because the code never expected that obscure field to be null.

The code was in "Transactional Reconciliation Service".

posts.text:
Big moment for Local AI!

running models locally always had one hard rule. if the weights didn't fit in GPU VRAM or unified memory, the model didn't work.

that rule is why running a 180B-class open model has meant buying a $10-20K workstation.

but this is about to change.

in the video below, i'm running Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B model, on an M4 Max with 64 GB of memory.

it runs in OpenCode at 56 tokens/sec, with a 2-bit quant and a 64k context.

this sounds impossible, but it works because of how today's open models are built.

they are sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. each layer holds many small sub-networks called experts, and a router picks only a few of them per token.

Qwen 3.8 Flash Next has 180B parameters, but only ~6B run on any given token. so ~97% of the model sits idle on every token, and local runners still kept all of it in VRAM.

SSD expert streaming fixes this. it keeps attention and the session's most-reused experts in fast GPU or unified memory.

everything else stays on the NVMe SSD, and the engine reads it only when the router picks it.

however, it's not as simple as it sounds. a naive version of SSD streaming crawls at a couple of tokens/sec, and there are four reasons why:

↳ a basic cache evicts experts the next few tokens need again.

↳ layer-by-layer disk reads leave the GPU and SSD waiting on each other.

↳ speculative decoding verifies several tokens at once, so each step touches more experts.

↳ long prompts flush the cache that decoding depends on.

Magnitude, an open-source inference engine launching today, solves all four together:

↳ it ranks experts by reuse and keeps the top ones in GPU memory, so most tokens never touch the disk.

↳ it peeks at upcoming tokens and prefetches their experts before the GPU stalls.

↳ it schedules direct NVMe reads across layers and bypasses OS swap entirely.

↳ during prefill, it reads each cold expert once per layer while the GPU computes, so long prompts don't wipe the hot cache.

streaming never writes to the SSD, so there's no flash wear. more RAM or VRAM still helps, since it keeps more experts hot.

on first launch, Magnitude profiles the hardware, predicts tokens/sec for each model before download, and tunes kernels for that exact chip. there are no flags to set.

it runs on Apple Silicon, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, or plain CPU, as a desktop app, CLI, or Docker image. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cline connect in one click, with an OpenAI-compatible API for everything else.

i think this is the biggest change to local inference since quantization. the limit on what runs at home moves from VRAM size to SSD speed.

a fast NVMe drive costs a fraction of a high-end GPU.

it's free, Apache 2.0 licensed, and fully local.

Check this out: https://github.com/magnitudedev/magnitude

(don't forget to star 🌟)

I also wrote a detailed article on how Magnitude automatically finds the best model to run on your device. The article is quoted below.
posts.why_viral: A 180B MoE running at 56 tok/s on a 64 GB M4 Max by streaming idle experts from NVMe instead of VRAM.
posts.why_it_matters: Magnitude is Apache 2.0 and plugs into Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Cline, so local 180B-class models no longer need a $10-20K box.
posts.newsletter_title: Magnitude streams sparse MoE experts from SSD so a 180B model runs on a 64 GB Mac.

posts.text:
Code Mode is an experimental new feature in Claude Code that can improve both speed and context efficiency when Claude needs to orchestrate multiple steps. Try it out and let us know what you think!

It enables Claude to perform multi-step tool calls by writing and running JavaScript. Rather than calling one tool at a time (e.g. Bash, Read, or Edit) and waiting to see the result before deciding what to do next, Code Mode allows Claude to write a simple script to run multiple commands in parallel, passing arguments and filtering outputs for subsequent tool calls to reduce context.

I'm excited about this work because Code Mode enables more efficient and streamlined multi-step coding flows. For example, rather than passing large amounts of raw search data into the context window or having to make a large number of sequential calls to perform the same refactoring across dozens of files, Claude can orchestrate these tasks programmatically in a single pass. 

Still, you will be able to interact with Claude as normal through natural prompts. And if you ever need to see the exact JavaScript that Claude generated, you can always use Ctrl+O to expand the collapsed Code rows in the transcript viewer.

One of the most exciting practical improvements from Code Mode is its ability to perform long-running operations, like running test suites or complex builds, as background processes. When Code Mode is running in either auto or bypassPermissions mode, scripts can run in the background for up to two hours. You can continue to interact with Claude and perform other work within the same session. The /tasks command provides complete transparency and control over background scripts.

Each tool call that is generated within a script is still governed by your current deny and ask permission policies, sandbox constraints, and PreToolUse hooks. Hooks can even be defined specifically for the REPL tool to inspect the generated JavaScript before running, or redact sensitive tokens from the output before reading it into the context. 

To enable Code Mode, just start your session with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 claude or set the environment variable in your ~/.claude/settings.json file.

Give it a try by running multi-file audits, batch edits, or any type of parallel search-and-filter operation. Code Mode is experimental and the team is actively iterating on it, so please run /feedback in your terminal to let us know what works well and where you hit any edges. 

Hope it's helpful!
